lessons.title: Study Session 1: Setting a Goal Worth Chasing

blocks.text: Introduction Chiamaka Obi opened the new financial year at an industrial supplies distributor in Nnewi to find her sales target was last year's number with a flat ten percent added, the same method her manager had used for as long as anyone on the team could remember, regardless of what had actually changed in the market that year. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the relationship between goal difficulty and task performance. Distinguish a vague or copied target from a specific, difficulty-calibrated goal. Apply a structured method for setting a goal that is both difficult and realistic. Recognise when a target has been set by habit rather than by genuine analysis. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Same Number, Plus Ten Percent Chiamaka Obi manages a sales territory for an industrial supplies distributor in Nnewi, and her new target for the year was calculated the same way it had been for as long as she could remember: take last year's number, add ten percent, done. It took her sitting down with the actual account data, new competitor activity in the region, and a major client's own expansion plans, to realise that flat percentage had nothing to do with what was actually achievable that year. 2.2 What Makes a Goal Actually Work In 2002, the researchers Edwin Locke and Gary Latham published a synthesis in American Psychologist reviewing 35 years of goal-setting research. Drawing on more than 400 studies, they found that specific, difficult goals produced higher performance than vague or easy goals in roughly 96 percent of trials, but crucially, that this effect depended on genuine commitment to the goal and on timely, relevant feedback along the way, not on difficulty alone. 2.3 Setting a Goal That Can Actually Hold Up Grounding a Target in Real Account and Market Data Building a target from actual account potential, known market changes and specific client plans, rather than from last year's number alone, gives a goal a foundation that can survive scrutiny. Making the Goal Specific, Not Just Bigger Stating precisely what the goal covers, which accounts, which products, over what period, rather than a single vague revenue figure, is what the Locke and Latham research found made a goal genuinely actionable. Building In a Feedback Point, Not Just an End Date Setting a specific checkpoint partway through the goal period to review progress keeps the goal connected to the kind of timely feedback the research found necessary for the difficulty effect to actually pay off. 2.4 Key Practices Ground a new target in actual account potential and known market changes, not last year's number alone. State a goal specifically, naming what it covers and over what period. Build at least one mid-period feedback checkpoint into every goal set. Question a target that was set by simply repeating last year's method unchanged. 2.5 A Worked Example: Chiamaka's Rebuilt Target Chiamaka rebuilt her own annual target from the ground up, factoring in her largest client's confirmed expansion plans, a new competitor that had entered two of her smaller accounts, and a realistic estimate of what her actual capacity allowed, arriving at a number meaningfully different from the inherited ten percent formula, and higher in some segments, lower in others. Her manager, sceptical at first, approved the revised target once he saw the account-level reasoning behind each figure, and a mid-year checkpoint Chiamaka had built in flagged one segment falling behind early enough to redirect effort before the year was lost. Chiamaka's actual selling skill had not changed from the year before. The number she was chasing had simply, for the first time, been built to match reality rather than habit. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Repeating a prior target with a flat percentage increase, without checking it against actual account and market conditions, produces a number that looks precise while meaning almost nothing. A goal has to be grounded in something real to be worth the effort of chasing it. 2.7 The Formula Had Never Actually Been a Plan Chiamaka's inherited target had looked like careful planning for years. It had simply been arithmetic, repeated long enough to be mistaken for a strategy. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a sales goal grounded in real account and market data rather than habit. Study Session 2 turns from setting the right goal to covering the right territory or accounts to actually reach it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a target you have been given or have set for yourself. Was it grounded in real data, or inherited from a prior period unchanged? 2. Build one mid-period checkpoint into a current goal of your own, naming a specific date and what you will review. Practical Output: Practical Output A rebuilt sales target for one real territory or account set, grounded in specific data, with one mid-period feedback checkpoint defined. 7.0 References and Further Reading Locke, E.A., & Latham, G.P. (2002). Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705 to 717. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Luke 14:28, on counting the cost before beginning to build a tower. Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:286, on Allah not burdening a soul beyond what it can bear.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose

blocks.text: Introduction Youssef Amrani discovered, while reviewing a colleague's departure, that an entire province his firm sold construction materials into in Tetouan had been quietly uncovered for nearly four months, not because anyone had decided to deprioritise it, but because nobody had ever formally reassigned it after the previous rep left. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the productivity impact of structured sales territory design. Distinguish deliberate territory coverage from coverage that simply happens by default. Apply a basic method for reviewing whether every account or area has a clear owner. Recognise when a coverage gap has gone unnoticed because no one was formally responsible for finding it. Rebalance territory or account assignments based on genuine workload and opportunity. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Four Months, No Coverage, No One Noticed Youssef Amrani manages regional sales operations for a construction materials firm in Tetouan, and reviewing coverage after a colleague's departure, he discovered an entire province had gone without an assigned salesperson for nearly four months. No formal decision had ever been made to drop that territory. It had simply fallen into a gap between one rep leaving and a replacement being hired, and nobody had checked in the meantime. 2.2 What Structured Territory Design Actually Achieves In 2005, the researchers Andris Zoltners and Prabhakant Sinha published a review in Marketing Science examining sales territory design, drawing on more than 1,500 project implementations across 500 companies. Their finding was that structured, deliberate territory alignment consistently improved sales productivity, but also that the combinatorial complexity of the problem and its personnel implications meant it could never be treated as a one-time, purely technical exercise completed once and then ignored. 2.3 Covering the Map on Purpose Maintaining a Single, Current Ownership List Keeping one clear, regularly updated record of which salesperson owns which territory or account prevents a gap like Youssef's from opening quietly whenever someone leaves or a role changes. Reviewing Coverage on a Fixed Schedule, Not Only After a Departure Checking territory ownership on a regular calendar, rather than only when a departure prompts a look, catches a gap opening before it has time to sit unnoticed for months. Rebalancing by Workload and Opportunity, Not Just Geography Reassigning territory based on genuine account potential and current rep capacity, rather than by geographic convenience alone, is closer to the deliberate design the Zoltners and Sinha research linked to real productivity gains. 2.4 Key Practices Maintain a single, current record of which salesperson owns which territory or account. Review coverage on a fixed schedule, not only when a departure prompts a look. Rebalance assignments based on genuine workload and account opportunity. Treat a newly vacant territory as an immediate reassignment task, not a background item. 2.5 A Worked Example: Youssef's Coverage Audit Youssef built a single master coverage list naming an owner for every territory and account, reviewed quarterly regardless of staffing changes, and set a rule that any vacancy triggered an interim reassignment within a week, even if only as a temporary measure until a permanent replacement was hired. The very next staffing change under the new system, a rep moving to a different role, was caught and reassigned within four days, compared to the four months the earlier gap had gone unnoticed. Youssef's actual product range and pricing had stayed exactly the same throughout both situations. The only thing that had changed was that coverage now had someone actively watching it, rather than assuming it would take care of itself. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Assuming territory coverage will remain intact by default, without a fixed schedule for actively checking it, allows a gap to open silently whenever staffing changes and go unnoticed for far longer than anyone would accept if they were actually looking. Coverage has to be actively maintained, not simply assumed. 2.7 The Gap Had Never Been a Decision Youssef's uncovered province had never actually been deprioritised by anyone. It had simply been forgotten, and forgetting, it turned out, could cost a territory just as much as a deliberate decision to abandon it. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to cover territory or accounts by deliberate, actively maintained design rather than by default. Study Session 3 turns from covering the right ground to building a forecast honest enough to plan around once that ground is covered.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a territory, account list, or area of responsibility in your own work. Is there a single, current record of who owns it? 2. Set a fixed schedule, such as quarterly, for reviewing coverage in your own work, and name the first review date. Practical Output: Practical Output A master coverage list naming an owner for every territory or account in one real sales team, with a fixed review schedule defined. 7.0 References and Further Reading Zoltners, A.A., & Sinha, P. (2005). The 2004 ISMS Practice Prize Winner, sales territory design: Thirty years of modeling and implementation. Marketing Science, 24(3), 313 to 331. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Nehemiah 3, on each family and worker rebuilding the section of the wall directly in front of their own house. Qur'an, Surah Al-An'am 6:165, on being made successors upon the earth with degrees of responsibility.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Building a Forecast That Can Be Trusted

blocks.text: Introduction Zawadi Mushi, who cares for her elderly mother alongside running sales operations for an agricultural inputs supplier in Arusha, noticed her monthly forecasts had missed in the same optimistic direction for six consecutive months before she finally pulled every past forecast into a single sheet to see the pattern plainly. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the accuracy of company sales forecasts compared to simple naive forecasts. Distinguish a genuinely accurate forecast from one that is simply biased in a consistent direction. Apply a method for checking a forecast's historical bias before trusting a new one. Recognise when optimism, not genuine uncertainty, is the main source of forecast error. Adjust a forecasting process to correct for a known, measured directional bias. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Wrong in the Same Direction, Six Times Running Zawadi Mushi manages sales operations for an agricultural inputs supplier in Arusha, and after a sixth consecutive month of finishing meaningfully below her own forecast, she compiled every monthly forecast and actual result from the past year into a single comparison sheet. The pattern was unmistakable once it was laid out: every single miss ran in the same optimistic direction, never once in the other. 2.2 What Actually Drives Forecast Error In 2000, the researchers Michael Lawrence, Marcus O'Connor and Bob Edmundson published a field study in the European Journal of Operational Research examining sales forecasting accuracy and processes across thirteen manufacturing organisations. Their finding was that company forecasts were not uniformly more accurate than a simple naive forecast based on recent history alone, and that most of the error came not from genuine unpredictability but from inefficiency and a systematic bias toward optimism in how forecasts were adjusted. 2.3 Correcting for a Known Bias Comparing Every Forecast Against Actual Results, Consistently Logging every forecast alongside its eventual actual result, month after month, is what makes a directional bias visible in the first place, rather than each miss being dismissed individually as an isolated surprise. Checking Whether a Naive Forecast Would Have Done Better Comparing a carefully constructed forecast against a simple projection of recent actual results reveals whether the extra effort in forecasting is actually adding accuracy or simply adding optimism. Applying a Correction Once a Bias Is Confirmed Adjusting future forecasts by the measured size of a confirmed historical bias, rather than trusting each new forecast at face value, turns a known weakness into something that can actually be corrected for. 2.4 Key Practices Log every forecast alongside its eventual actual result to make any pattern visible. Compare forecasts periodically against a simple naive projection of recent results. Apply a measured correction once a consistent directional bias is confirmed. Treat a forecast miss as data about the forecasting process, not just about that single month. Recheck an applied bias correction every few months, since a market shift can change its size. 2.5 A Worked Example: Zawadi's Bias-Corrected Forecast Zawadi calculated the average size of her six-month optimistic miss and began subtracting that measured amount from her raw monthly forecast before submitting it, treating the correction as a standing adjustment rather than a one-time fix, while continuing to log new results to check whether the bias held steady or shifted. Her corrected forecasts over the following quarter landed within a much narrower margin of actual results than any of the prior six months had managed, close enough that her regional manager began planning inventory and staffing around her numbers with real confidence for the first time. Zawadi's actual sales performance had not improved in that period. The forecast describing that performance had simply, finally, been telling the truth about it. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating each forecast miss as an unrelated, isolated surprise, without ever comparing misses against each other for a pattern, allows a genuine and correctable directional bias to persist indefinitely. A bias that is never measured can never be corrected. 2.7 The Forecasts Were Never Random Zawadi's six missed months had never actually been six unrelated strokes of bad luck. They had been the same mistake, made quietly and consistently, until she finally laid them all out where the pattern could no longer hide. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to detect and correct a directional bias in sales forecasting rather than treating each miss as unrelated. Study Session 4 turns from forecasting overall results to choosing the specific numbers that actually predict them.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent forecast or prediction you made in your own work. Did it miss, and if so, in which direction? 2. Log your own forecasts and actual results for the next month, and compare the result against a simple projection of recent history. Practical Output: Practical Output A forecast log comparing at least three past forecasts against actual results, with a calculated bias correction to apply going forward. 7.0 References and Further Reading Lawrence, M., O'Connor, M., & Edmundson, B. (2000). A field study of sales forecasting accuracy and processes. European Journal of Operational Research, 122(1), 151 to 160. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Genesis 41:29-30, on Joseph interpreting the seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. Qur'an, Surah Yusuf 12:47-48, on Joseph's counsel to plant during the years of abundance in preparation for the years of hardship.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Chiamaka's sales target was calculated as last year's number plus a flat ten percent, regardless of market changes. What did this reveal?
options: The formula was a sound and sufficient planning method
A target set by habit rather than by genuine account and market analysis may bear little relation to what is achievable
Flat percentage increases always undershoot true potential
Chiamaka's territory had no real growth opportunity
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Setting a Goal Worth Chasing) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Locke and Latham's 2002 research, what did specific, difficult goals produce compared to vague or easy goals?
options: Consistently worse performance across nearly all trials
Higher performance in roughly 96 percent of the more than 400 studies reviewed
No measurable difference in performance
Improved performance only when goals were kept easy
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Setting a Goal Worth Chasing) before continuing.

quiz.q: What did the same research identify as necessary for the difficulty effect to actually pay off?
options: Nothing further; difficulty alone was sufficient
Genuine commitment to the goal and timely, relevant feedback
Avoiding any feedback until the goal period ended
Setting goals without informing the person responsible for them
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Setting a Goal Worth Chasing) before continuing.

quiz.q: An entire province went uncovered for four months after a rep's departure, with nobody noticing. What did this reveal?
options: The province had genuinely been deprioritised on purpose
Territory coverage can quietly lapse without a deliberate, actively maintained system for tracking ownership
Construction materials sales require no territory management
Youssef's firm had too many salespeople for its territory
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Zoltners and Sinha's 2005 research, what did structured territory alignment consistently achieve?
options: No measurable effect on sales productivity
Improved sales productivity, though never as a one-time, purely technical exercise
A reduction in overall account potential
Complete elimination of personnel-related complications
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend maintaining to prevent a coverage gap?
options: No formal record; informal awareness is sufficient
A single, current record of which salesperson owns which territory or account
A record updated only once a year
Separate, uncoordinated lists kept by each individual salesperson
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose) before continuing.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Choosing the Numbers That Actually Matter

blocks.text: Introduction Kojo Mensah tracked eleven separate activity metrics for every salesperson on his team at a beverage distributor in Ho, calls made, visits logged, samples dropped, and more, until a simple year-end comparison showed almost none of those eleven numbers actually predicted which reps closed the most business. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about using predictive analytics to evaluate salesperson performance. Distinguish an activity metric from a metric that genuinely predicts results. Apply a method for testing which tracked numbers actually correlate with outcomes. Recognise when a busy-looking scorecard is measuring motion rather than results. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Eleven Numbers, Almost None of Them Useful Kojo Mensah manages a sales team for a beverage distributor in Ho, and for over a year, his weekly team reports tracked eleven separate activity figures per salesperson. Running a simple year-end comparison against actual closed revenue, he found that most of those eleven numbers showed almost no relationship to which reps had actually performed best, while two figures he had barely paid attention to turned out to matter a great deal. 2.2 What Predictive Analytics Actually Found In 2020, the researchers Nuno Calixto and João Ferreira published a study in Applied Sciences applying predictive analytics to three years of data from 594 salespeople at a global freight forwarding company. Their finding was that specific behavioural and outcome metrics classified salesperson performance categories far more reliably than raw activity counts, meaning simply tracking more numbers, or the most visible ones, was not the same as tracking the numbers that actually predicted results. 2.3 Finding the Numbers Worth Tracking Testing Each Tracked Metric Against an Actual Outcome Comparing each individual metric already being tracked against actual closed results over a meaningful period reveals which numbers genuinely predict performance and which simply measure activity for its own sake. Dropping a Metric That Shows No Real Relationship to Results Removing a tracked figure once it has been shown to have little bearing on outcomes frees up attention for the smaller set of numbers that actually matter. 2.4 Key Practices Test each currently tracked metric against actual closed results over a meaningful period. Keep tracking a metric only once it has shown a genuine relationship to outcomes. Drop a metric that shows no real predictive relationship, regardless of how easy it is to collect. Revisit which metrics matter periodically, since what predicts results can shift over time. 2.5 A Worked Example: Kojo's Trimmed Scorecard Kojo ran a year of team data against actual revenue outcomes and found that call count and sample drops, the two metrics his team had always discussed most in meetings, showed almost no relationship to who actually closed business, while follow-up speed after a client enquiry and the number of repeat visits to an existing account both tracked closely with performance. He cut the weekly report down from eleven tracked figures to four, keeping the two newly confirmed predictors alongside two others that had also shown a genuine relationship, and team meetings shifted from reciting a long list of activity numbers to discussing what those four figures actually meant. Kojo's team had not become more active in any dramatic new way. They had simply stopped being measured, and praised, for activity that had never actually been moving the outcome. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Tracking a long list of activity metrics simply because they are easy to count, without ever checking whether they relate to actual outcomes, buries the few numbers that genuinely matter under a pile of numbers that do not. More tracked metrics is not the same as better tracked metrics. 2.7 The Busiest-Looking Numbers Were the Least Useful Ones Kojo's eleven metrics had never been meaningless exactly. Most of them had simply been measuring motion, and motion, it turned out, had never been the same thing as the results everyone actually cared about. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to test tracked metrics against actual outcomes and keep only the ones that genuinely predict results. Study Session 5 turns from choosing the right numbers to reviewing them on a regular, structured cadence.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a metric you track in your own work. Have you ever checked whether it actually relates to an outcome you care about? 2. Compare one metric from your own tracking against actual results over the past few months to see whether a real relationship exists. Practical Output: Practical Output A trimmed scorecard for one real sales team, keeping only metrics tested and confirmed to relate to actual outcomes. 7.0 References and Further Reading Calixto, N., & Ferreira, J. (2020). Salespeople performance evaluation with predictive analytics in B2B. Applied Sciences, 10(11), Article 4036. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 27:23, on knowing well the state of your flocks and giving attention to your herds. Qur'an, Surah Al-Hashr 59:18, on every soul looking to what it has sent ahead for tomorrow.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: The Honest Performance Review

blocks.text: Introduction Halima Bello, who rebuilt her career in sales administration in Zaria after being displaced from her home region some years ago, dreaded her monthly review meetings with her manager, sessions that consisted almost entirely of a single number read aloud, met with either brief approval or open irritation, and nothing resembling an actual conversation. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the consequences of failing to make quota. Distinguish a review that treats a miss as information from one that treats it only as a verdict. Apply a structure for a performance review that goes beyond a single pass or fail number. Recognise when a review process is producing anxiety without producing any useful next step. Design a review cadence appropriate to a team's actual selling cycle. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Number Read Aloud, Nothing Else Halima Bello handles sales administration for a wholesale textiles firm in Zaria, and her monthly reviews with her manager had followed the identical format for well over a year: a single revenue figure stated aloud, a brief reaction, and the meeting ended within minutes. Whether the number was above or below target, nothing about why, or what to do next, was ever actually discussed. 2.2 What Missing a Quota Actually Costs In 2004, the researchers Charles Schwepker and David Good published a study in the Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing examining the consequences of quota failure. Their finding was that failing to make quota carried measurable, concrete consequences for a salesperson's performance, income and the firm's overall revenue, underscoring that a missed target is not a minor event to be glossed over quickly, but one significant enough to warrant a genuine, structured review rather than a brief, purely reactive comment. 2.3 Building a Review Worth Having Asking Why Before Reacting to the Number Starting a review by asking what specifically drove a result, rather than reacting to the headline figure first, turns the conversation from a verdict into an investigation worth having. Ending Every Review With a Specific Next Step Closing a review with at least one concrete action to try before the next one, rather than simply restating the target, gives the number somewhere useful to go afterward. Matching Review Frequency to the Actual Selling Cycle Setting a review cadence that fits how long a typical deal actually takes to close, rather than an arbitrary calendar interval, keeps each review meaningful instead of catching the same deal mid-progress every time. 2.4 Key Practices Ask what specifically drove a result before reacting to the headline number. End every review with at least one concrete, specific next step to try. Match review frequency to the team's actual selling cycle, not an arbitrary interval. Treat a missed target as a starting point for a conversation, not the end of one. Document the specific reasoning behind each review, not only the final figure. 2.5 A Worked Example: Halima's Restructured Review Halima proposed a revised review format to her manager: five minutes discussing what specifically had driven the month's result, five minutes identifying one concrete change to try next, and a shift from a strict monthly cadence to one aligned with her team's typical six-week sales cycle, so each review actually captured a meaningful chunk of completed work rather than an arbitrary calendar slice. The first review under the new format surfaced a specific, fixable delay in how quotes were being approved internally, a problem the old format's single number had never once revealed in over a year of monthly meetings. None of that credit belonged to any change in Halima's own work. The review process itself had finally been asked to do more than announce a verdict. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Reducing a performance review to a single number stated and reacted to, without asking what drove it or defining any next step, produces anxiety around the number while leaving the actual underlying cause completely unexamined. A verdict without an investigation rarely changes anything. 2.7 The Number Had Never Been the Whole Story Halima's monthly figure had never actually been wrong to report. It had simply, for a long time, been treated as the entire conversation, when it had only ever been the opening line. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion This study session covered how to run a performance review that investigates a result rather than only announcing it. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning that same review data into the basis for genuine coaching.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a review or evaluation you have experienced. Did it investigate what drove the result, or only state it? 2. Design a revised review format for your own work, including a specific next-step question to close with. Practical Output: Practical Output A revised performance review structure for one real team, including a cause-focused opening question, a defined next step, and a review cadence matched to the actual selling cycle. 7.0 References and Further Reading Schwepker, C.H., & Good, D.J. (2004). Understanding sales quotas: An exploratory investigation of consequences of failure. Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing, 19(1), 39 to 48. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Lamentations 3:40, on examining and testing our ways and returning to what is right. Qur'an, Surah Al-Isra 17:14, on one's own self being sufficient as a reckoner against oneself this day.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Coaching From the Numbers, Not the Gut

blocks.text: Introduction Emmanuel Rugamba had coached the same salesperson on the same general theme, be more assertive with prospects, for nearly a year at an insurance brokerage in Huye, a piece of advice that felt right based on a general impression, until he actually pulled that salesperson's call data and found assertiveness was not the issue at all. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research identified as the core constructs of effective sales coaching. Distinguish coaching based on a general impression from coaching grounded in specific performance data. Apply a structure for building a coaching conversation directly from tracked performance data. Recognise when coaching advice has been repeated from habit rather than drawn from current evidence. Build trust in a coaching relationship by grounding feedback in specific, checkable data. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Year of the Same Advice, Aimed at the Wrong Problem Emmanuel Rugamba manages a sales team at an insurance brokerage in Huye, and for nearly a year he had coached one particular salesperson toward the same general goal: be more assertive with prospects. Finally pulling that salesperson's actual call and follow-up records, Emmanuel found assertiveness in the initial conversation was not weak at all. The real pattern was a long delay before any follow-up call after a prospect's first meeting, often five or six days, by which point interest had visibly cooled. 2.2 What Effective Sales Coaching Is Actually Built On In 1998, the researcher Gwyneth Rich published a study in the Journal of Personal Selling & Sales Management identifying the core constructs of effective sales coaching. Her finding was that effective coaching rested on three identifiable elements, supervisory feedback, role modeling and the salesperson's trust in the manager, with feedback grounded in real, specific performance data forming the foundation the other two constructs depended on to actually mean anything. 2.3 Coaching From What the Data Actually Shows Reviewing Actual Records Before Forming an Opinion Pulling a salesperson's actual tracked data, call logs, follow-up timing, conversion points, before settling on what to coach toward prevents a general impression from quietly hardening into repeated, misdirected advice. Grounding Feedback in a Specific, Checkable Example Pointing to a specific instance drawn from the data, rather than a vague overall impression, is what the Rich research linked to feedback a salesperson could actually trust and act on. Modeling the Specific Behaviour the Data Points To Demonstrating the exact behaviour the data suggests needs to change, rather than only describing it in the abstract, reflects the role-modeling construct the research identified as a distinct, necessary part of effective coaching. 2.4 Key Practices Review a salesperson's actual tracked data before forming a coaching opinion. Ground every piece of feedback in a specific, checkable example from that data. Model the specific behaviour the data points to, not only a general description of it. Revisit coaching advice periodically to confirm it still matches current data, not a past impression. Build trust by showing a salesperson the data behind a piece of coaching, not just the conclusion. 2.5 A Worked Example: Emmanuel's Data-Grounded Coaching Shift Emmanuel brought the actual follow-up timing data into his next coaching conversation, showing the salesperson the specific pattern of five and six day delays across several recent prospects, then worked through, together, a same-day follow-up habit and modeled exactly how a same-day check-in call might sound. Follow-up timing across that salesperson's next set of prospects dropped to within a day in nearly every case, and the conversion rate on those leads rose noticeably within the following two months. Emmanuel's year of assertiveness coaching had not been wasted out of laziness. It had simply been aimed at a problem that the data, once he finally looked at it, showed had never actually been the real one. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Repeating the same coaching advice based on a general impression, without ever checking it against a salesperson's actual tracked data, risks coaching toward a problem that does not exist while the real one goes unaddressed indefinitely. A year of well-intentioned advice aimed at the wrong target changes nothing. 2.7 The Advice Had Been Sincere. It Had Also Been Aimed at Nothing. Emmanuel's assertiveness coaching had never been bad advice in the abstract. It had simply never been checked against the one thing that could have told him, months earlier, that it was solving a problem his salesperson did not actually have. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to ground coaching in specific tracked data rather than a general impression. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Sales Compensation and Incentive Design, the next course in Pathway 39.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a piece of advice or feedback you have given or received repeatedly. Was it ever checked against actual data? 2. Pull one real set of performance data for someone you coach or manage, and identify one specific, checkable example to ground your next conversation in. Practical Output: Practical Output A data-grounded coaching plan for one real team member, naming a specific pattern drawn from tracked data and one behaviour to model directly. 7.0 References and Further Reading Rich, G.A. (1998). The constructs of sales coaching: Supervisory feedback, role modeling and trust. Journal of Personal Selling & Sales Management, 18(1), 53 to 63. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Chronicles 12:32, on the men of Issachar who understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Qur'an, Surah Al-Asr 103:1-3, on exhorting one another to truth and to patience.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Kojo tracked eleven activity metrics, but most showed no relationship to actual closed revenue. What did this reveal?
options: More tracked metrics automatically produce better management insight
Tracking a metric because it is easy to count does not mean it actually predicts performance
Activity metrics are always more useful than outcome metrics
Kojo's sales team was fundamentally underperforming
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Choosing the Numbers That Actually Matter) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Calixto and Ferreira's 2020 research, what did specific behavioural and outcome metrics do compared to raw activity counts?
options: They performed worse at classifying performance
They classified salesperson performance categories far more reliably than raw activity counts
They showed no measurable difference from activity counts
They could only be applied to freight forwarding companies specifically
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Choosing the Numbers That Actually Matter) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing with a metric that shows no real relationship to outcomes?
options: Continuing to track it regardless, for consistency
Dropping it, regardless of how easy it is to collect
Tracking it even more closely to find a hidden pattern
Replacing it with an identical metric under a different name
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Choosing the Numbers That Actually Matter) before continuing.

quiz.q: Halima's monthly reviews consisted of a number stated aloud with no further discussion. What did this reveal?
options: This format was thorough and sufficient for performance management
A review reduced to a single number produces anxiety without examining the cause or defining a next step
Halima's actual performance was consistently poor
Monthly reviews are inherently unnecessary
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (The Honest Performance Review) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Schwepker and Good's 2004 research, what did failing to make quota carry?
options: No measurable consequences of any kind
Measurable, concrete consequences for performance, income and firm revenue
Consequences only for the salesperson's manager, not the salesperson
Purely psychological effects with no financial impact
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (The Honest Performance Review) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing before reacting to a headline result?
options: Nothing further; the number should be the sole focus
Asking what specifically drove the result
Immediately assigning blame to the salesperson
Comparing the result only to competitors' figures
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (The Honest Performance Review) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Chiamaka's sales target was calculated as last year's number plus a flat ten percent, regardless of market changes. What did this reveal?
options: The formula was a sound and sufficient planning method
A target set by habit rather than by genuine account and market analysis may bear little relation to what is achievable
Flat percentage increases always undershoot true potential
Chiamaka's territory had no real growth opportunity
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Setting a Goal Worth Chasing) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Locke and Latham's 2002 research, what did specific, difficult goals produce compared to vague or easy goals?
options: Consistently worse performance across nearly all trials
Higher performance in roughly 96 percent of the more than 400 studies reviewed
No measurable difference in performance
Improved performance only when goals were kept easy
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Setting a Goal Worth Chasing) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What did the same research identify as necessary for the difficulty effect to actually pay off?
options: Nothing further; difficulty alone was sufficient
Genuine commitment to the goal and timely, relevant feedback
Avoiding any feedback until the goal period ended
Setting goals without informing the person responsible for them
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Setting a Goal Worth Chasing) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: An entire province went uncovered for four months after a rep's departure, with nobody noticing. What did this reveal?
options: The province had genuinely been deprioritised on purpose
Territory coverage can quietly lapse without a deliberate, actively maintained system for tracking ownership
Construction materials sales require no territory management
Youssef's firm had too many salespeople for its territory
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Zoltners and Sinha's 2005 research, what did structured territory alignment consistently achieve?
options: No measurable effect on sales productivity
Improved sales productivity, though never as a one-time, purely technical exercise
A reduction in overall account potential
Complete elimination of personnel-related complications
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend maintaining to prevent a coverage gap?
options: No formal record; informal awareness is sufficient
A single, current record of which salesperson owns which territory or account
A record updated only once a year
Separate, uncoordinated lists kept by each individual salesperson
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Planning Territory or Account Coverage on Purpose) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Zawadi's forecasts missed in the same optimistic direction for six consecutive months. What did this reveal?
options: Each month's miss was an unrelated, random event
A consistent directional bias had been present the whole time, only visible once the pattern was laid out together
Her actual sales performance had been steadily declining
Forecasting was not a worthwhile exercise for her role
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Building a Forecast That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Lawrence, O'Connor and Edmundson's 2000 research, what did company forecasts fail to consistently outperform?
options: A fully automated computer model
A simple naive forecast based on recent history alone
Competitor sales figures
Government economic projections
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Building a Forecast That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What did the same research identify as the main source of forecast error?
options: Genuine, unavoidable market unpredictability
Inefficiency and a systematic bias toward optimism in how forecasts were adjusted
A complete absence of any historical data
Errors in how actual results were recorded
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Building a Forecast That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

options: More tracked metrics automatically produce better management insight
Tracking a metric because it is easy to count does not mean it actually predicts performance
Activity metrics are always more useful than outcome metrics
Kojo's sales team was fundamentally underperforming
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Choosing the Numbers That Actually Matter) before continuing.
